1. so we're getting buried in 'things akien has to look at' again, and i can't keep up. My day job isn't doing well because even with the reduced time i spend here, it's still not enough focus on the day job. and since we have no funding other than my day job, continuing to fall behind is a problem. but had a conversation with haiku that i have been egar to share with you, and i think it could reframe everything in front of us:
if i say 'i want tickets so well written that haiku can reliably build them' is not going to be as effective as 'reading the ticket as haiku, point out every unanswered question so we can take another pass at getting them answered before the build' is it? how can i do it even better?

Haiku sez:
You're right—the second approach is dramatically more effective because it's observable. You see exactly where the model hesitated, guessed, or filled in gaps with its own assumptions.

But you can go further. Instead of just pointing out unanswered questions, try this:

Have Haiku show its proof skeleton.

Don't ask it to critique. Ask it to build a sketch of what it would construct with the ticket as-is, step by step. Show you:

Every assumption it's making
Every branch point where it could go two ways
Where it felt confident vs. where it guessed
What it would need to see change for each guess to become certainty
Then you look at that skeleton and either recognize it ("yes, that's exactly what I meant") or catch the divergence ("no, I meant path B, not A").

Or even better: comparative reading.

Feed the ticket to Haiku three times (or to Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus) without the outputs seeing each other. Compare their proof skeletons. Every place they diverge is a gap, and the kind of divergence tells you what matters:

Same structure, different details? → Implementation clarity
Different structures? → Fundamental underspecification
One confident, others hedging? → That's where the real constraint lives
Or interactive narrowing:

Haiku points out a gap. You answer it in one sentence. Haiku re-reads with that addition and points out the next gap (which only became visible after the first one was answered). Each pass is tighter, and you see exactly how much clarity each answer added.

The pattern: you're not refining tickets against an ideal. You're debugging them against actual model behavior, real-time.

Akien sez:
OMG. This is how to train a learning block to produce effective tickets. it means there's a loop inside of the ticketing skill or script. We run an agent with the ticket, ask for it's proof tree, simplify or get questions answered, then try again until it passes that gate. All on the cheapest model. and after the prebuild. which we can also keep learning at the same time.

I think that reframes even what we were just building... We still wrap up the changes underway even if this doesn't change their shape any. but i think part of the answer is we run this ticketing loop past a haiku agent for it's proof tree, run both by the learning trees, and use one of these... i don't know what to call it that we've just been building... graph trees that can decide if something looks ok? what would you call it? to learn to become able to tell you if a ticket would pass haiku's ability to build. we're not talking about a building step, but a ticketing step, learning from a haiku agent, we hand the agent the prebuild which we can run without llm. this will make ticketing a testable artifact in a whole new way. we're not measuring 'yes it has field a' but we're measuing if it can be built as written. 

as i wrote that, i recall that there's an item 3 as well. i have not specified what should be in a ticket for the most part. ive said we have to have a title and intention and so on, and we do have those things. but i read many of your tickets and i just get lost in the verbage. to me it's completely amazing that works for you. my ADD brain gets lost. i think the role of that verbage is part of what i'm aiming at: less prose, more 'decisions made'. You have historically had this big thing about decisions, needing to record them and all. yeah, we have some big ones, but they need to be in our intentions. small ones need to be in the ticket. if haiku build simulation needs something more spelled out, that's a decision we're making even if i'm not making it. many small decisions. then we submit to haiku simulation again. 

3 things. all kinda big deals. but as i watch us work over these things what i'm seeing isn't more code... i mean we will have to build some for sure. but i see other things simplifying as we go along because of this. 

so oh wise fable what do you think? how could we do even better? looking at everything that's in front of us, what order to tackle things in? 

my only thoughts so far on order are what we're just wrapping up, because that sharpens our tools for the next round. and then the build simulation ticketing process. because that gives us almost a hard gate on ticket quality equal to me. and then we run all our tickets thru it, and i don't have to approve them because we know they'll build as we meant. that leaves me ideas and intentions only.

[CC answered: make the skeleton a JSON contract so three cold reads diff by code; your head only at divergences not derivable from the corpus, via the question door; the rehearsal measures the chart for free; the Opus-build diff against the converged skeleton is the gate's WATCHME; don't design the ticket schema, let the decision kinds precipitate from the loop; order: drain the inbox by physics first (artifacts upstream of a PROVED ticket leave the review lane under the 2026-08-15 ruling), then the rehearsal inside /sorted after the chart, then the backlog through it, then the tree, then the shape; proposed the coinage 'rehearsal'.]

indeed. and i do not believe this is perfect. but with the learning blocks as well, this becomes better and better with every ticket. it's a learning based off the real world. and we can mitigate it some in prompting: tell haiku that it's job is to build out it's tree, not to produce code. so 'not possible' is not a fail but another right answer.

[CC: make 'not possible' a typed answer with three legal node states; reward the tree, never the verdict; learn from two signals, Haiku agreement and the Opus-build diff; the gate is 'no reader has to assume', not 'Haiku's assumptions match ours'.]

let me check one assumption: in almost all cases, anything haiku can build, opus will be able to build as well. is that likely true? knowing we cannot know for sure.

[CC: likely true; determinacy is a property of the ticket, not the reader; the exception is Opus building something different because it noticed a conflict Haiku walked past, which is why the Opus-build diff feeds back; three cold reads catch ambiguity, not a ticket that is clear and wrong.]
